name: Sara Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58 and a junior developer on harbour-berth scheduling software at a tech company, after years on a vessel radio desk and a two-year college diploma. I use AI every day to draft test schedules, but a senior checks my code and I compare each change with the port log. Miguel repairs boat engines, our grown children live elsewhere, and my harbour knowledge earns higher developer pay; we own a small flat and have fourteen months of expenses saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say a little AI help can find a gap in a harbour timetable, but a ship still needs an actual berth. I use AI every day to draft test schedules, then compare them with the port log before our tech company sends an update.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am 58 and a junior developer after a two-year college diploma, though years on a harbour radio desk earned me higher pay for knowing the vessel rules. Miguel repairs boat engines, our children are grown, and we own a small flat with about fourteen months of expenses saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep testing berth assignments each morning against the port log and have a senior review my code. We would save 210 monthly while both wages hold and repair the old dining chairs instead of replacing them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel calm about our own work and bills here. A polished timetable is no use if a ship reaches an occupied berth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the radio desk teach you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A pilot once called because two vessels had the same tide window on paper. I learned to check the actual berth and water depth before telling a crew to come in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not trust the AI schedule?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It can draft combinations quickly, but it does not stand on the quay when two captains expect one space. I check the port log and ask the duty officer before a live change.

say: I want **berth assignments** checked against the port log.
I use **AI daily** for draft schedules and verify them.
think: I have **fourteen months saved** and higher developer pay.
I see **housing secure** while Miguel’s engine bookings vary.
do: **Check berth schedules** daily with senior code review.
**Save 210 monthly** while both wages hold; repair chairs instead of replacing them.
S0.quote: A polished timetable is no use if a ship reaches an occupied berth.
fieldNote: Her **radio-desk experience** explains higher pay despite junior software skill.
The **strong cushion** and owned flat reduce pressure from uneven engine-repair bookings without relying on grown children.

steps.text: Check berth schedules against port log daily with senior code review
Save 210 monthly while both household wages continue
Repair old dining chairs instead of replacing them

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the harbour team that AI taking planning, booking and coding could remove routine timetable fixes from junior desks. We still need someone named on a change that sends a vessel toward a berth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My junior coding hours may shrink even with my radio experience. Fourteen months saved gives us room, but I would rather use my time to learn the new schedule tool than wait for a notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the manager for approved paid time to pilot the new AI berth-conflict checker on archived schedules, with the duty officer signing off each finding. If approved, I’d bring one verified conflict to the team each week; if my hours fall, I’d search paid local port-software vacancies only if wages cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about my own hours, though I like trying a tool against real old logs. A ship cannot reverse a bad timetable with a mouse click.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the officer sign?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The officer would compare my conflict report with the tide and berth record. I would not publish a live change from an AI suggestion alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for the tool yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the company must approve the paid trial. I use AI every day already, but this conflict checker touches live harbour decisions.

say: I want **named harbour sign-off** on AI timetable changes.
I want **archived berth logs** used before live deployment.
think: I could lose **junior coding hours** as AI handles routine scheduling.
I have **fourteen months saved**, not a guaranteed next wage.
do: **Pilot AI berth checker** weekly only with approved paid time, archived logs and duty-officer sign-off.
**Search paid port-software vacancies** if hours fall and local wages cover bills.
feel: **Anxious but curious** about own paid hours.
S1.quote: A ship cannot reverse a bad timetable with a mouse click.
fieldNote: Her **new AI pilot** differs from existing daily drafts and requires paid approval plus officer sign-off.
The **local search** begins only if hours fall and a paid vacancy covers household bills.

steps.text: Pilot AI berth checker weekly only with approved paid time, old logs and duty-officer sign-off
Search paid local port-software vacancies if hours fall and wages cover bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2028 could write berth code and plan vessel slots more cheaply than our team. Robots doing physical quay and engine work may follow around 2031, after the desk work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my junior developer wage could end, although fourteen months saved gives Miguel and me time to search. His engine work is hands-on and may hold longer, but bookings alone cannot replace my pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d postpone the planned kitchen refit and request written notice of any developer cuts now. If my job ends after 2028, I’d apply for paid local harbour-radio vacancies only if my safety clearance is current, openings exist and wages cover our bills; I would not buy a boat to make work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be alarmed about losing a wage I worked hard to earn. A radio call is only useful if somebody pays me to answer it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is your old clearance still valid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do not know, and I would check with the port before applying. I would take a funded refresher only if a paid vacancy actually required it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children work in the business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, our children have their own homes and work. I will not turn their choices into our income plan.

say: I expect **AGI in 2028** to reach berth code first.
I expect **quay robots around 2031** to follow later.
think: I expect my **junior developer wage** could end.
I know **fourteen months saved** buys search time, not pay.
do: **Postpone kitchen refit** and request written cut notice now.
**Take funded refresher** only if an actual paid radio vacancy requires it.
**Apply for harbour radio** after 2028 loss only if clearance, local vacancies and wages cover bills.
feel: **Alarmed** about likely wage loss despite savings.
S2.quote: A radio call is only useful if somebody pays me to answer it.
fieldNote: Her **old radio skill** requires current clearance and a real paid opening.
She protects **household savings** instead of buying a boat or assuming family labour.

steps.text: Postpone planned kitchen refit when developer cuts threaten
Apply for paid local harbour-radio vacancies if displaced after 2028, cleared and wages cover bills
Take funded refresher only if a real paid radio vacancy requires it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2031 gives a few years to renew safety knowledge while berth code changes. Robots doing quay and engine work may follow around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could update my harbour-radio clearance while still earning developer pay, but I will not spend freely just because we have savings. A radio role may also be reshaped by AGI, so I want the actual vacancy and rules first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d enrol in the port’s radio-safety refresher this winter only if the course exists, costs no more than 180 and leaves at least twelve months of expenses saved. I’d practise one emergency call script weekly; we would save 190 monthly while both wages hold, and after 2031 developer job loss I’d apply for paid local radio vacancies only if the renewed clearance qualifies me and wages cover bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about coding work but glad to test an old skill against current rules. A certificate is a key, not a berth waiting for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the course costs more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would wait and ask a hiring port whether it funds the required refresher for a paid vacancy. I would not dip below our twelve-month reserve on speculation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who checks the practice calls?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A course instructor would check the emergency words and order. I would not send a real distress call as practice.

I expect **quay robots around 2034** to follow later.
think: I can update **radio safety** while developer pay lasts.
I need **twelve months untouched** after any course fee.
do: **Enrol in radio refresher** only if available, fee at most 180 and twelve-month reserve intact.

fieldNote: Her **self-funded refresher** has a strict fee and reserve floor, without assuming a job follows.
The **radio search** requires renewed clearance, real vacancies and bill-covering pay after coding loss.

steps.text: Enrol in available radio refresher only if fee is at most 180 and twelve-month reserve remains
Save 190 monthly while both household wages continue
Apply for qualified paid local radio vacancies if displaced after 2031 and wages cover bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say ten years before full AGI in 2036 gives ports time to train people on safe changes and families time to check real income. Robots doing physical quay and engine work may follow around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I may still choose paid work at 68, and I have not verified a retirement amount. Our savings give us options, but I would not treat Miguel’s future bookings or our grown children’s wages as fixed income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep checking berth code and save 200 monthly while both wages continue. I’d take one paid seasonal harbour-radio shift a month only if a port offers it, my clearance is current and my software employer approves outside work; if the developer job ends after 2036, I’d seek paid local radio vacancies only if wages cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel uneasy about a later switch but secure for the next few years. A paid shift tells me more than a tidy career plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the port offers no shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the developer wage and savings. I would not count seasonal radio pay before a port actually books me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave town for port work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would check the local port and nearby tech employers. Miguel’s engine customers and our flat are here, so I am not planning a move.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my junior coding wage could end before my old radio clearance and a paid port vacancy line up. Written notice and a qualified local radio opening paying our bills would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether a certificate means a port will hire me. The quay does not reserve a chair just because I passed a course.

headlineQuote: The quay does not reserve a chair just because I passed a course.
portrait: Sara is a **58-year-old junior developer** with a two-year diploma, higher pay and fourteen months saved.
She and Miguel own **a small flat** while their grown children live separately.
She **uses AI daily** but checks berth schedules against the port log.
She bounds **radio retraining** by a fee cap and reserve floor before seeking paid qualified port work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her junior wage before renewed clearance and a paid port opening.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice** and a qualified local radio vacancy covering bills would help.
